articles.title: ‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risks
articles.summary: Andy Burnham’s focus on immediate domestic problems leads some to fear issue has dropped off government’s radar. Towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, his senior ministers, alarmed by the latest developments in artificial intelligence, began drawing up plans for a new AI safety law.
body: They ordered a review of existing legislation to see what powers they already had, according to those briefed on the plans, and were exploring whether they could force the world’s most advanced technology companies to submit their products for safety testing before launching them.
In the midst of the political chaos that engulfed the former prime minister as he fought to remain in office, however, the plans fell by the wayside.

Now, after two weeks in which the world has been warned there is a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans”, and King Charles has warned about its potentially destructive capabilities, the government’s attention has turned again to what to do about AI.

Andy Burnham, Starmer’s successor in Downing Street, has said relatively little about the technology in the past, and in one of his first acts in office he scrapped the department that had been leading the legislative work.

articles.title: BrewDog creditors owed £190m will not be paid in full, say administrators
articles.summary: There are ‘insufficient funds’ to pay unpaid wages, tax owed to HMRC and overdue bills, accountants say. Accountants picking over the remains of BrewDog, the “punk” beer company that collapsed earlier this year, have said that creditors who are owed about £190m will not be paid back.
body: In an update on their progress, administrators at AlixPartners warned there were “insufficient funds” to pay debts in full related to unpaid wages, tax owed to HM Revenue and Customs, and overdue bills from other businesses.

Earlier this year, the US cannabis and drinks company Tilray snapped up BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars in a rescue deal for about £33m, agreed after the brewer fell into administration.
But the deal in March did not includemost of BrewDog’s chain of bars, with 38 closing and 440 staff losing their jobs.
The collapse rendered worthless the investments of 200,000 “equity punks”, the small investors who crowdfunded the business.

articles.title: The best peel-and-stick wallpapers that appeal to every budget, according to interior designers
articles.summary: Adding a touch of zhuzh to the home has never been easier – these alternatives to traditional wall decor are simple to apply and low mess. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things. I’ll come clean. I’ve spent years coveting wallpapers.
body: Peel-and-stick seemed like the perfect antidote – but before I invested, I checked in with a handful of experts about the best wallpaper to use, how to choose it, and most importantly, how to put it up.

After listening to all the tips, deciding on my patterns and spending two afternoons sticking paper to the walls of my Brooklyn apartment, I can assure you that yes, you really can do it – and it looks just as good as traditional wallpaper.

The pros: a lower up-front cost and faster installation. You can also cleanly remove it without damage. “Think of it like a rug for your walls. You don’t have to worry about scratching furniture or smudging the walls because you’re covering them,” said Suzette Conrad, digital creator and marketing manager at the home remodeling firm Bolt Builders.

Of course, there are some downsides. “Peel and stick is great for renters or anyone who wants the option to remove or swap out their wallpaper,” said Ann Marie Winkler, principal interior designer at Huron Interiors. “However, if the adhesive isn’t re-positionable, it can actually be tougher to install since it’s harder to correct placement once it’s on the wall.”

articles.title: Felicity Green obituary
articles.summary: Innovative journalist who as fashion editor of the Daily Mirror brought the latest 1960s looks to millions of readers. Felicity Green made a career on tabloid newspapers in their most masculine era when, after secretaries and tea-trolley ladies went home, whole buildings could be as all-male as a…
body: Green, who has died aged 100, knew how extraordinary her value had been to the group. The Daily Mirror, at its peak of five million-plus readers, besides being a household’s source of news and sport, offered families access to what we would now call pop culture – showbiz, celebrity and especially style. Newspapers were a main advertising medium through the 1950s, 60s and 70s, and agencies yearned for content to attract women, who controlled household purchases, and young people, a new market for discretionary spending.

Green was working at the ad agency WS Crawford in 1955 when Hugh Cudlipp, editorial director of the Mirror Group, asked for her opinion on the Women’s Sunday Mirror, a new paper he had launched to appeal to demographics the advertisers desired. She detailed its faults fiercely; he recruited her to its staff. The paper did not last, but Green moved to his Sunday Pictorial (later the Sunday Mirror) and then the Daily Mirror, with overall responsibility for women, and as “Felicity Green on the fashion scene”.

articles.title: New York Knicks MVP Jalen Brunson Accidentally Made His Runway Debut
articles.summary: While the 2026-2027 NBA season doesn’t start until late October, New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson is keeping busy.
body: Jordan Clarkson may have walked in Willy Chavarria’s spring 2027 menswear show this summer, but he’s not the only New York Knicks player to give modeling a try.

Jalen Brunson made his unexpected runway debut yesterday at the Rookie Kids × Macy’s Runway on Broadway fashion show. The Knicks captain’s daughter, Jordyn, hit the runway in a tiny Knicks jersey—dad’s number 11, awww —festooned with feathers, a white bow headband, and a pair of little blue-and-white sneakers. But while she was already holding mom Ali’s hand on the catwalk, it seemed that Jordyn was more keen for her dad to join her, rather than merely watch from the front row.
Brunson gamely hopped up from the crowd. With each parent holding a hand, Jordyn was far more content to finish her walk.
Jalen Brunson walked the Rookie Kids runway with his daughter, Jordyn, and wife, Ali.

articles.title: Tove Lo Has a Lot of Feelings and No Solutions
articles.summary: The pop pioneer talks about her sixth album “Estrus,” returning to Sweden to find herself again, and why there will always be a reason to disappear on the dance floor.
body: When I speak to Tove Lo, she has just landed in New York. She’s DJing a New York Fashion Week party before heading to Nashville, where she will begin preparing to get back onstage. It has, somehow, been almost three years since she finished touring Dirt Femme, and she has missed it more than she realized.

There is the discipline of it, she says: building a set with her band, training to do something extreme night after night. But there is also its opposite. “The unleashing you have to do of mind, body, soul, and voice is so powerful,” she tells me. When she finally returned to the rehearsal room, something clicked. “I was like, Oh wow, this is that thing …I need this to feel leveled.”

That tension of discipline and abandon, control and release is the right place to begin with Tove Lo—real name Ebba Tove Elsa Nilsson—who came to pop with her neon-glowing 2014 debut Queen of the Clouds, a heady, radical-feeling soundtrack for feeling both vulnerable and voracious on the dance floor—a genre in itself these days. Her sixth album, Estrus, out today, represents a more mature inflection of honesty from the sad-girl-pop pioneer.
